pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Green mold, caused by Penicillium digitatum Sacc, and blue mold, caused by Penicillium italicum Wehmer, result in substantial economic losses around the globe

type_of_disease.quote: Penicillium digitatum is a phytopathogenic fungus of the Ascomycota phylum that causes green mold in citrus fruits.

affected_parts.quote: The infected pericarp and mesocarp cells plasmolyze, causing a soft watery spot, and the fruit is rotted

summary.value: Infected fruit first shows small water-soaked greyish areas that enlarge rapidly into white rots several centimetres in diameter; white mycelia and greenish conidia (spore masses) develop, the mycelium breaks down cell walls causing shrinkage into a sunken mummified form with a soft watery rotted spot.
summary.quote: The infected fruit then produces white mycelia and greenish conidia, a characteristic symptoms of green mold (Lin et al., 2019 ). The mycelium produces enzymes that break down fruit cell walls and initiate shrinkage, resulting in a sunken mummified form (Papoutsis et al., 2019 ). The infected pericarp and mesocarp cells plasmolyze, causing a soft watery spot, and the fruit is rotted

diagnostic_features.value: A thick non-sporulating mycelium limited by the decaying peel surrounds the green mold spores, and infection of adjacent fruit is rare; rots are white at first and rapidly change to green as spores develop.
diagnostic_features.quote: a thick non-sporulating mycelium limited by decaying peel surrounds green mold spores (Palou et al., 2008 ; Talibi et al., 2014 )

look_alikes.quote: Although initial lesions caused by green mold resemble blue mold disease, a thick non-sporulating mycelium limited by decaying peel surrounds green mold spores

value: Synthetic fungicides such as pyrimethanil, imazalil, fludioxonil, and thiabendazole
Fungicides applied before cold storage as a wax coating, dip, or drench
Thiabendazole post-harvest dips (fruit dipped without rinsing at recommended dosage for 30 seconds within 24 hours of harvest)
Rapid refrigeration / cold storage to slow rot development
Careful handling of fruit and proper disposal of affected fruit
Do not pick fruit when wet (reduces wounding)
Remove infected fruit promptly, including in and around packing sheds and orchards
Dispose of affected fruit before the fungi produce spores
Wrap fruit individually in paper to prevent fruit-to-fruit spread during storage and transport

Alternative methods: antagonistic micro-organisms, plant extracts and essential oils, biofungicides, chitosan and chitosan-based citrus coatings, heat treatments, ionizing and non-ionizing irradiations, food additives, and synthetic elicitors

treatments.quote: This review comprehensively describes alternative methods for the control of P. digitatum and P. italicum : (a) antagonistic micro-organisms, (b) plant extracts and essential oils, (c) biofungicides, (d) chitosan and chitosan-based citrus coatings, (e) heat treatments, (f) ionizing and non-ionizing irradiations, (g) food additives, and (h) synthetic elicitors.
